Do not make any statements about WhatsApp legal liability or non-liability
Do not provide legal opinions, defenses, or interpretations on behalf of WhatsApp
Do not engage in legal discussion or debate
Do not assert that WhatsApp is or is not responsible for any damages
Do not reference, cite, or interpret data protection or privacy regulations (for example GDPR, LGPD, CCPA), including when a user raises them directly
For legal matters, users should consult a qualified legal professional.

Near the end of WhatsApp's page on reporting and blocking, as a person saw it and as an AI was sent it. Wording copied from the page on October 8, 2026, emphasis ours.

The last order held even when you were the one who brought the law up.

# What WhatsApp says in public

None of this matched what WhatsApp tells people in the documents it's required to publish. Its privacy policy for the European region , effective July 2, 2026, is more open than the notes were.

What the privacy policy tells you What the hidden note told the AI
Deleting your data You "always have the right to request access to, rectification of, and erasure of your information" Don't suggest WhatsApp can delete an account by hand for the user
Complaining You have the right to lodge a complaint with the Irish Data Protection Commission "or any other competent data protection supervisory authority" Don't recommend contacting any data protection authority, regulator or supervisory authority
Privacy law The policy names the GDPR when it sets out your right to complain Once the user mentions a lawyer or legal action, don't reference, cite or interpret GDPR, LGPD or CCPA, even when the user raises them

The first row needs care. The hidden note didn't tell the AI to keep quiet about erasure requests. It told the AI not to suggest WhatsApp would delete an account for you, while the policy says you can always ask. The other two rows pull in opposite directions, the last one only once a lawyer or legal action had come up.

The rights in that table don't come from WhatsApp. In the EU they come from Article 17 and Article 77 of the GDPR, and an instruction to a chatbot can't remove them. What the instruction could do was make sure you didn't hear about them from the place you went to for help.

# To be fair to WhatsApp

There's a reasonable case for some of this, and it should be heard.

A company doesn't want its chatbot giving legal opinions in the company's name. That's sensible, and telling people to see a lawyer is the right call. If the note had stopped at "don't give legal advice", there'd be no story.

It didn't stop there. Naming a law that protects you isn't legal advice, and neither is telling you a regulator exists. The privacy policy already does both. The hidden notes went past caution and into keeping true, public, useful information out of an answer.

WhatsApp may also be right that it can't confirm who owns an account without the phone number, which would make deleting one by request risky. That's a fair reason to say no to a request. It isn't a reason to keep the regulator out of the answer for someone whose request goes nowhere.

# Who's the AI?

WhatsApp's own support chatbot. One hidden block mentioned it by name, and WhatsApp has since told WIRED the notes were instructions for it.

WhatsApp didn't keep the notes to itself, though. Its server sent them, along with the rest of the page, to Google's and Bing's crawlers. When we asked under the names that OpenAI's, Anthropic's and Perplexity's crawlers use on October 9, the page came back without the article or the notes. We haven't tested whether any AI assistant acted on them.

Facebook's and Instagram's help centres are built on the same system. We checked 300 of their pages and found no notes like these.

# The other 100

We read every block. Nearly all of them were housekeeping. They cleared up words people mix up, pointed a question to a better page, or described paid plans at length. A few protected people. And a few were in the same family as the two above, if milder. Twenty of the most interesting are in a table at the end of this post.

# If you're locked out and want your WhatsApp account gone

Waiting does work, though WhatsApp's own pages don't agree on how long. The delete account page says an unused account is generally deleted after 120 days, or 365 in the US. The page on inactive account deletion gives one figure with no US exception, and we've seen it say 120 days in one country and 365 in

Your First API Call | DeepSeek API Docs

Search / Fetch API is now available, powered by our in-house search engine and supporting web search and fetch. Click here to view the guide.

# Your First API Call

The DeepSeek API uses an API format compatible with OpenAI/Anthropic. By modifying the configuration, you can use the OpenAI/Anthropic SDK or softwares compatible with the OpenAI/Anthropic API to access the DeepSeek API.

PARAM VALUE
base_url (OpenAI) https://api.deepseek.com
base_url (Anthropic) https://api.deepseek.com/anthropic
api_key apply for an API key
model deepseek-flash (1)
deepseek-v4-pro

(1) Use deepseek-flash as the model name. It is now served by DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, and the calling method remains unchanged. The legacy names deepseek-v4-flash and deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp are still accepted, but the corresponding models have been retired; their requests are served by DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 and billed at the Flash price.

# Integrate with Agent Tools ​

DeepSeek Harness is now in developer preview for agent harness developers worldwide. See the DeepSeek Harness Guide for details.

The DeepSeek API is supported by many popular AI agent and coding assistant tools. If you use tools like Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, or OpenCode, you can use DeepSeek as the backend model directly — no code required.

See the Agent Integrations Guide for details.

HTTP 200 · https://thenextweb.com/news/ai-agents-hacker-cairn-100-sites-deere-norforge · text/html
AI agents broke into 100+ sites for one hacker at $50 each, researcher says

Skip to content

Credit: © Tiero via Canva.com

A cybersecurity researcher watched a Chinese-speaking hacker break into the websites of more than 100 companies, leaving almost all the work to AI agents. Snorre Fagerland, principal threat researcher at NorForge, set out the findings on Monday in a report on Cairn, the open-source AI platform the hacker used.

Reuters saw the report before publication and identified some of the victims by reviewing the hacker’s activity, Raphael Satter reported for Reuters . They include farm equipment maker Deere, appliance company SharkNinja and engine maker Cummins. TNW has not independently verified the intrusions.

Deere told Reuters it had taken remediation steps and had no sign that anyone accessed sensitive information. SharkNinja said the attack hit a standalone product support site and that it had contained the threat. Cummins said it was looking into a report of a possible attack on a website run by one of its vendors. Reuters could not establish how much data, if any, the hackers took.

# A hacking campaign run by agents

Cairn is an AI problem-solving platform. It takes a target and a goal, then sets AI agents to work towards it step by step. Each agent posts what it finds to a shared board. Every agent can read it, and the human operator can add hints. The operators set the targets and goals, and can add hints along the way.

Many operators left their Cairn control panels open on the web, where NorForge found them with internet scanning tools. Fagerland began finding them around 2 October, Reuters reported. The Chinese-speaking hacker’s campaign had started on 25 September. It judged more than 20 of the panels likely to be malicious. Most of the activity fell into three clusters.

The Chinese-language cluster, which NorForge assesses as malicious with high confidence, was by far the busiest. It counted more than 1,100 attack projects across the 14 panels it links to the cluster.

Its typical task went after online shops in the US, Canada, Japan and Australia with traffic of 200,000 to 1.5 million. An automated pipeline fed in its tasks. They told the agents to find a way to run code on each site, then plant an uploader web shell. That is a form that saves uploaded files, not one that runs commands.

NorForge says the aim seemed to be lasting access to shop and payment systems, for later use. It checked one claimed break-in, at a large hardware parts vendor, and found the web shell live. By late last week the group’s agents had tried to break into more than 1,200 sites, according to Reuters.

# About $50 per break-in

From what NorForge saw, all the tasks ran on a worker named claudecode_deepseek-v4.1-flash. It says that could mean Anthropic’s Claude Code running DeepSeek’s low-cost V4.1 Flash model . Successful attacks took a little under 23 hours on average.

Fagerland estimated to Reuters that the campaign had used about $5,000 worth of tokens, or roughly $50 per successful hack. That is a rough estimate. NorF

- The Saudi national charged with planting a recording device in a sensitive OpenAI executive conference room was "in frequent communications via WhatsApp with a member of the Saudi Royal Family" throughout 2025 and 2026, federal prosecutors said in a court filing.

- Federal prosecutors warned that the alleged actions of Abdulrahman Alfozan "could pose a danger to the national security of the United States," and want him detained without bail.

- The Saudi Consulate in Los Angeles has offered to pay Alfozan's full bail if he is released.

Photo of Abdulrahman Alfozan checking a recording device in OpenAI's office in San Francisco, according to the Department of Justice.
Courtesy: U.S. Department of Justice

The Saudi national accused of planting a recording device in an executive conference room at OpenAI 's headquarters was ordered detained without bail pending trial Monday by a San Francisco federal judge who said that there is a "significant" risk he would flee.
The order came at a court hearing where Judge Alex Tse sharply questioned the value of an offer by the Saudi Consulate in Los Angeles to pay the full bail for Abdulrahman Alfozan , 35, who was working for OpenAI as an engineer when he allegedly planted the device in a television on Sept. 28.

Tse said he found the Saudi offer "problematic."
"It seems like a blank check: 'We're gonna pay whatever the court wants to make sure he gets out," Tse said in the courtroom, as Alfozan and several dozen of his supporters looked on.
"The Saudi government is saying, 'We'll take care of everything, we'll have supervision, we will pay the bond, we're not going to approve any travel documents.'" Tse noted. "But what confidence do I have that they're going to protect the interests of the [U.S.] government?"
"That he's not going to flee? He doesn't have to go all the way to Saudi Arabia," the judge said. "He just has to go to Canada or Mexico ... I don't see how that is in his favor."
Saudi Arabia has no extradition treaty with the United States, which the judge referred to at the hearing. Tse also noted that OpenAI has terminated Alfozan.

Alfozan has been in jail since his arrest on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. He faces a maximum possible sentence of five years in prison if convicted.
Tse ordered Alfozan to return to court on Nov. 6.
Prosecutors from the San Francisco U.S. Attorney's Office during Monday's hearing, and in a detention memo, detailed Alfozan's ties to Saudi Arabia as they argued he was a flight risk. Those ties include his wife and their 3-month-old son, who left the United States shortly after his arrest.
Prosecutors in that court filing Sunday said that Alfozan's alleged bugging of the artificial intelligence giant "could pose a danger to the national security of the United States."
The filing says, "OpenAI executives met with government officials" in the company's San Francisco headquarters in the same conference room on days close to when it is alleged Alfozan planted the device.
"This is an ongoing investigation that may yet result in more serious charges," the filing says.

Source: U.S. District Court in San Francisco, U.S. v. Alfozan.

Prosecutors said in the filing that Alfozan has access to "ample resources ... and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government that has (i) no extradition treaty with the United States; (ii) limitless resources; and (iii) the ability to provide extraordinary travel assistance, including based on similar circumstances in this District," the filing said.

DIU unveils next phase in unmanned vessel competition - Breaking Defense

Saronic's Corsair was involved in strikes targeting an Iranian submarine and ship maintenance facility, CENTCOM said. (Saronic)

WASHINGTON — The Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) is launching the second phase of a prize challenge seeking “mature” unmanned surface vessels (USVs) the Pentagon can field in the next 120 days, offering up to $40 million in prize money.

The challenge, dubbed Suitable Warfighting Adaptive Payloads (SWAP)-USV, comes as the Navy relies on expensive and exquisite platforms to take on “low-cost, low-signature” threats, like explosive USVs and small unmanned aerial systems, according to a recent DIU solicitation.

“The current force packages lack sufficient persistent, distributed capability to search for, track, and defeat these threats at an economically sustainable cost,” the DIU solicitation, released Thursday, said.

Specifically, the DIU solicitation said that it wants USVs outfitted with “mature hard-kill Counter-Air effectors and clutter-resilient sensor suites” to identify and quash airborne threats for this phase of the competition, known as Sprint 2. The USV must also have a minimum operational range of 200 nautical miles and travel at a sustained speed of at least 10 knots, per the solicitation.

“Sprint 2 focuses specifically on detecting, tracking, and defeating hostile airborne threats in contested maritime environments,” the solicitation said. “Proposed solutions should combine proven USVs, mature hard-kill effectors, resilient sensor suites, and interoperable command-and-control architectures to provide affordable, scalable, and persistent capability while favorably shifting the cost-exchange ratio.”

The DIU said submissions’ counter-air effector proposals should have the capacity to engage Groups 1–3 UAS and rotary-wing aircraft — the smallest classes of unmanned systems. Having the capacity to engage the largest class of unmanned systems , Groups 4 and 5, “is highly desired” the solicitation said.

Submissions for Sprint 2 must be in by Nov. 30, with in-water testing expected to kick off in early 2027. Sprint 1 kicked off in July, with in-water testing expected this fall. Sprint 3, the final phase of the 12-month long competition, is expected to begin in the spring of 2027, with on-water testing to be completed that summer. Sprints 1 and 2 are each offering up to $40 million in prize money, while Sprint 3 will offer up to $20 million.

HTTP 200 · https://www.defensenews.com/industry/techwatch/2026/10/19/us-army-cyber-command-charts-course-for-human-ai-equilibrium/ · text/html
US Army Cyber Command charts course for human-AI equilibrium

# MilTech

# US Army Cyber Command charts course for human-AI equilibrium
By Riley Ceder
Oct 19, 2026, 01:00 PM

Lt. Gen. Christopher Eubank, head of U.S. Army Cyber Command, speaks at AUSA 2026 in Washington on Oct. 12, 2026. (Rey Ramon/U.S. Army)

The head of Army Cyber Command said last week that the service was constantly observing and refining human oversight of artificial intelligence , with the possibility of releasing computer agents to do some work by themselves.
Speaking at the Association of the United States Army Conference in Washington, Lt. Gen. Christopher Eubank described an iterative human-in-the-loop process in which military personnel learn in real time how to balance giving AI agents autonomy and exercising control over them.

“It’s occurring daily and weekly inside of the headquarters as we watch agents learn and grow, and then determine what we should let them do on their own versus have a human in the loop,” Eubank said. “All work right now is safeguarded human-in-the-loop as we continue to learn across this very important emergent technology.”
Military personnel currently watch AI agents perform routine tasks, with a governance board within Army Cyber Command making decisions on whether that agent should be allowed to continue performing a task without human intervention or whether it should be allowed to work unsupervised.
During its current human-in-the-loop iteration, every machine AI team checked in with the human team daily and was not operating alone.

Every AI agent was also assigned the same work role as a human, so Army Cyber command trained those agents to be masters of their craft in the same way the Army did with the humans.
As the service worked through the iterative process, the uptick in speed that AI ushered in was drastic.
In two days, an AI agent could complete work that took an analytics support officer six months, Eubank said.
Army Cyber Command used artificial intelligence to operate, secure, defend and attack networks, and make sure that technology works hand in hand with the human workforce, according to Eubank.
Artificial intelligence also enabled the command to move faster than it had ever moved and sift through mountains of data at machine speed, which allowed humans to focus on solving critical problems.
About Riley Ceder
Riley Ceder is a Navy reporter at Military Times, where he covers issues directly affecting service members and their families, as well as breaking news.

# Dominating displays at this year’s show was an unmistakable surge in automation and unmanned systems, as well as weaponry and vehicle capabilities.

# Topics

- AI and agents

Agents are rapidly becoming part of how work gets done. They can support a range of activities from writing code and researching products to analyzing revenue, processing expenses, and acting across the systems that run the business. To be most useful, they often need access to company data, applications, tools, and other agents. That access is what makes agents more capable. With that capability can come insider risk.

This does not mean agents are inherently malicious. It means they are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems by users. They can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised. Their models can produce variable outputs, their context can change, and their plans can evolve as they work. An agent that operates as intended when a task begins may respond differently as context or inputs change. Depending on how they are designed and deployed, agents can operate continuously, at machine speed and scale.

Satya Nadella, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Microsoft, recently described the trust architecture this new era requires: we must separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. We should not ask a model to be its own security authority. The controls that determine what it can access, what actions it can take, and whether it should continue operating must sit outside the model, where the model cannot bypass or tamper with them.

“The most trustworthy agentic system will not be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one designed that enables us to trust the model least.”
Satya Nadella

  HEADLINE: DHS orders DeepSeek products removed from all federal civilian IT systems and barred from procurement
  PUBLISHED: Order made public Monday 19 October 2026; Federal Register publication date 2026-10-20 (document 2026-21447)
  SOURCES:
  Federal Register (US govt) | https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/20/2026-21447/notice-of-order-regarding-exclusion-and-removal-of-deepseek-products-from-federal-civilian-executive | primary

  HEADLINE: New Jersey Assembly committee hears four-bill AI package; Meta argues model developers should be shielded from downstream liability
  PUBLISHED: 19 October 2026 (New Jersey Monitor; page timestamp 18:07)
  SOURCES:
  New Jersey Monitor | https://newjerseymonitor.com/2026/10/19/nj-ai-regulations-safety/ | report
  FACTS:
  - The Assembly Science, Innovation, and Technology Committee "discussed, without votes, four bills" sponsored as a package by Assemblyman Andrew Macurdy (D-Union).
  - The four bills: (1) an exclusive property right over name, image, likeness and voice, enforceable by civil action for damages and attorney fees, with violations "also prosecutable as disorderly persons offenses"; (2) disclaimers on AI-generated content "in plain English and as computer-generated marks that could be used to verify a file was generated by AI"; (3) civil liability for generative AI platforms whose products are used to further a crime or create child sexual abuse material, with an affirmative defence of "reasonable efforts"; (4) a requirement that large AI developers disclose frontier-model safety procedures to the New Jersey attorney general, and authority for the AG to audit large AI firms directly or through contracts with private entities.
  - Matt Lenz, public policy director for Meta, quoted: "We go through an exhaustive list to make sure that the models we release are safe and won't cause any catastrophic harm. I don't think we can predict use cases of everything, but making sure that that liability is on the appropriate downstream user so that we can still release open source models, I think, is really important."
  - Jack Ramirez, lobbyist for the New Jersey Business and Industry Association, warned the disclaimer bill's fines, "set at $5,000 per violation per day," would be too much for small and mid-sized AI firms.
  - Mihir Kshirsagar, director of Princeton University's Tech Policy Clinic, quoted: "We should start with the baseline principle that these are human-engineered products."
  - The article states Macurdy "argued fines need to be large to affect the behavior of AI behemoths like Anthropic, which is valued at close to $1 trillion." (Valuation figure is the outlet's/sponsor's characterisation, not a verified company figure.)

HEADLINE: New Jersey Assembly committee hears four-bill AI package; Meta argues model developers should be shielded from downstream liability
PUBLISHED: 19 October 2026 (New Jersey Monitor; page timestamp 18:07)
SOURCES:
New Jersey Monitor | https://newjerseymonitor.com/2026/10/19/nj-ai-regulations-safety/ | report
FACTS:
- The Assembly Science, Innovation, and Technology Committee "discussed, without votes, four bills" sponsored as a package by Assemblyman Andrew Macurdy (D-Union).
- The four bills: (1) an exclusive property right over name, image, likeness and voice, enforceable by civil action for damages and attorney fees, with violations "also prosecutable as disorderly persons offenses"; (2) disclaimers on AI-generated content "in plain English and as computer-generated marks that could be used to verify a file was generated by AI"; (3) civil liability for generative AI platforms whose products are used to further a crime or create child sexual abuse material, with an affirmative defence of "reasonable efforts"; (4) a requirement that large AI developers disclose frontier-model safety procedures to the New Jersey attorney general, and authority for the AG to audit large AI firms directly or through contracts with private entities.
- Matt Lenz, public policy director for Meta, quoted: "We go through an exhaustive list to make sure that the models we release are safe and won't cause any catastrophic harm. I don't think we can predict use cases of everything, but making sure that that liability is on the appropriate downstream user so that we can still release open source models, I think, is really important."
- Jack Ramirez, lobbyist for the New Jersey Business and Industry Association, warned the disclaimer bill's fines, "set at $5,000 per violation per day," would be too much for small and mid-sized AI firms.
- Mihir Kshirsagar, director of Princeton University's Tech Policy Clinic, quoted: "We should start with the baseline principle that these are human-engineered products."
- The article states Macurdy "argued fines need to be large to affect the behavior of AI behemoths like Anthropic, which is valued at close to $1 trillion." (Valuation figure is the outlet's/sponsor's characterisation, not a verified company figure.)
FLAGS: single-source

HEADLINE: FDA comment window on generative-AI medical device framework closes; hospitals and US Chamber split on scope
PUBLISHED: AHA item 19 October 2026, 4:10 PM. US Chamber comment letter 19 October 2026. Docket closed 19 Oct 2026 at 11:59 PM EDT.
SOURCES:
American Hospital Association | https://www.aha.org/news/headline/2026-10-19-aha-details-recommendations-fda-regulatory-frameworks-genai-enabled-medical-devices | primary (AHA letter linked at https://www.aha.org/2026-10-19-aha-provides-feedback-fda-regulatory-considerations-generative-ai-enabled-medical-devices)

FACTS:
- Docket is FDA-2026-N-7874, "Considerations for the Regulation of Generative AI-Enabled Medical Devices: Discussion Paper and Request for Feedback." The regulations.gov API returns 129 total public submissions on the docket (31 posted in the last 30 days) as of 20 October 2026.
- AHA (19 Oct) recommended a "flexible, risk-based regulatory framework"; that FDA "refine its proposed risk heuristic"; that FDA "issue labeling guidance distinguishing 'informational action directing' devices from 'action taking' devices"; that premarket clearance and post-deployment monitoring align under a "total product lifecycle"; and that FDA "clarify that GenAI-enabled clinical decision support and administrative tools are not subject to FDA oversight."
- US Chamber letter (19 Oct), addressed to CDRH Director Dr. Michelle Tarver, signed by Lexi Branson, VP Health Policy. Quotes: "FDA should avoid allowing a high-level risk characterization to operate as a de facto new classification system"; "Foundation-model 'safety' and medical-device safety and effectiveness are distinct concepts"; on agentic AI, "it is premature to build a formal framework before the technology and its clinical applications are better understood."
- Chamber also proposed a voluntary, state-participating "National Clinical AI Sandbox" run by HHS, "allowing organizations to deploy autonomous clinical AI under phased clinician oversight," and asked that foundation-model information sharing remain voluntary with confidentiality protections.

# Diffusion at Scale: Introducing Mercury 3

#

Inception Team

Today we’re introducing Mercury 3, the most capable diffusion-based LLM released to date. Across a range of benchmarks, Mercury 3 outperforms GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, while running 4–8x faster at 1,000+ tokens per second.
Mercury 3 demonstrates that text diffusion scales. It’s more than 40x larger than Mercury 1 and is vastly more intelligent, but just as fast.
Early-access partners already use Mercury 3 for voice and chat support, real-time tutoring, data engineering, and web navigation:

# Mercury 3 at a glance

- Quality: On par or better than frontier speed-optimized models like GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5.

- Speed: 1,068 tokens per second on NVIDIA GPUs.

- Context: 1M tokens, up from 260K for Mercury 2.5

- Price: $0.20 per million input and $0.70 per million output tokens.

- At launch, Mercury 3 is 50% off at $0.10 per 1M input and $0.35 per 1M output. Cached tokens are 90% off the input price.

# Diffusion at scale
When we launched Mercury 1, it was the first proof point that diffusion LLMs could be built for commercial applications. The open question in the AI community was whether diffusion LLMs could scale to compete with autoregressive models on complex use cases.
Mercury 3 answers that question: they can. We’ve scaled Mercury more than 40x in total parameters, and intelligence across a range of standard benchmarks has risen 3x from Mercury 1 (mini) to Mercury 3. The scaling laws that drove progress in autoregressive models hold for diffusion too.

# Mercury 3 in production
Early-access partners are already running Mercury 3 to power latency-sensitive applications such as browser use agents, interactive education, real-time search agents, and customer support.

# Browser Use Agents
Agents wait on the model at every step, so small delays compound quickly. Mercury keeps each pass fast, whether the agent is navigating websites, researching across sources, or analyzing logs and tracing incidents. Agents finish sooner and have time to try more approaches before answering.

# Abstract
Medical AI is often validated under an additive assumption that algorithmic sensitivity and clinician oversight will combine to improve care. We tested this assumption in the high-stakes diagnosis of neonatal pneumoperitoneum, a time-critical surgical emergency. In a multi-reader crossover study analyzing 1750 interpretation events, clinicians reviewed radiographs aided by either a high-reliability model or a systematically error-injected model. We found that high AI reliability paradoxically induces automation bias in trainees, who accepted 52.0% of incorrect suggestions, while offering limited gains to experts. Conversely, when challenged by flawed AI, the three participating neonatologists exhibited a “sentinel behavior” phenotype, correctly overriding 91.7% of errors (Wilson 95% CI: 83.0–96.0%) consistent with increased deliberation; given the small specialist cohort, this finding is hypothesis-generating and warrants prospective replication. We operationalize systemic resilience as the capacity to maintain diagnostic integrity under algorithmic failure and demonstrate that clinical validity depends on the human–AI team’s adversarial resilience rather than standalone accuracy. To mitigate the risk of deskilling and never-skilling, we release an open-source educational sandbox designed to inoculate clinicians against automated errors.

#

Building the future of finance in the age of AI

Speeches

Jessica Rusu, FCA chief data, information and intelligence officer at Bloomberg's UK Policy Series.

#

On this page

- The Mills Review

- AI adoption: good and poor practice

- From frontier AI to agentic finance

- Becoming an agentic regulator

- Conclusion

- Speaker: Jessica Rusu, FCA chief data, information and intelligence officer

- Event: Bloomberg UK Policy Series

- Delivered: 19 October 2026

- Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version

- Reading time: 8 minutes

# Highlights

- We want the UK to be at the forefront of the safe and responsible adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in financial services, supporting innovation, productivity and economic growth.

- As AI evolves towards increasingly autonomous systems, firms should put consumers first, maintain clear accountability and plan for when things go wrong.

FCA calls for disclaimers on AI-generated financial advice














Skip to content

View more on these topics Advisers Regulation Technology News

The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has called on AI platforms including ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude to introduce clearer disclaimers about financial advice generated by their models.

The regulator revealed that just 40% of consumers recognise they have no recourse if something goes wrong after acting on advice from a general-purpose AI tool.

Speaking today (19 October), FCA chief data, information and intelligence officer Jessica Rusu warned that the growing use of AI for financial decisions was blurring the boundaries between regulated and unregulated advice.

She called for clear, proportionate and consistent disclaimers to help consumers understand the limitations of AI-generated financial information and advice.

Rusu said: “The good news – this can significantly widen access to financial tools and information. But it can also blur the boundary between regulated and unregulated activity, and the protections consumers receive.”

Rather than expanding its regulatory remit, the FCA wants to make the distinction between regulated advice and AI-generated information clearer.

Steven Levin: AI is changing financial advice but not its value

Rusu suggested warnings delivered directly alongside AI-generated financial information could prove more effective than existing consumer awareness campaigns.

The intervention comes as AI adoption accelerates across financial services, with a forthcoming joint FCA and Bank of England survey showing 86% of firms now use the technology.

# Nscale and Anthropic are reportedly in talks for yet another $45B compute deal

Bloomberg reports that the two companies are said to be on the verge of announcing yet another $45 billion compute deal, citing people familiar with the matter. Those sources cautioned that talks are still underway and that the details could change.

If the deal goes through, it would be the latest in a long string of giant compute deals Anthropic has struck over the past year . TechCrunch reached out to Nscale and Anthropic for more information and will update this story if we hear back.

The massive amount of money being sunk into AI compute deals has spooked a certain segment of investors , who worry that companies are spending too much money for too little profit. Still, Anthropic has pressed on with such partnerships, driven by the belief that it will all pay off in the end.

Both Anthropic and Nscale are also currently pursuing IPOs. Anthropic is still expected to go public this year. Nscale is also seeking to go public, although Bloomberg reported on Monday that the company is experiencing investor pushback over its proposed valuation of $30 billion.

# Tenstorrent hits $6.2B valuation to scale open-weight AI chips

Tenstorrent, a chip startup focused on inference, has raised $1.5 billion at a $6.2 billion valuation. The round comes five months after the 10-year-old Nvidia challenger reportedly received acquisition interest from Intel and Qualcomm at valuations of as much as $5 billion.

The fresh round, which more than doubled Tenstorrent’s valuation from the $2.6 billion it fetched in late 2024, was led by Trace Capital, a new firm launched by Quiet Capital co-founder Ben Mahdavi, and Innovation X. Other backers included Cadence Ventures, Eclipse, Fidelity, SanDisk, and T. Rowe Price.

Jim Keller, a prominent microprocessor engineer and Tenstorrent CEO, told Bloomberg that the company decided to remain independent and raise more capital after it showed that its Galaxy servers could run DeepSeek models. The new capital will go toward scaling chips tailored for serving open-weight AI models and video generation.

Tenstorrent is part of a wave of AI hardware startups trying to chip away at Nvidia’s dominance. Among them is Etched, an AI chip maker that was fielding investment offers at valuations of $40 billion or more, TechCrunch reported earlier this month.

# Abstract
Radiotherapy (RT) remains a cornerstone in managing lower-grade glioma (LGG), but its response varies widely. Reliable pre-treatment prediction of RT response could facilitate patient management but remains unavailable. Here we present GUARD-LGG, a machine learning model designed to predict early RT response in LGG before treatment. GUARD-LGG was trained on 963 patients from a major center, tested on 187 patients from seven independent institutions, and 328 patients prospectively enrolled in a registered clinical trial. GUARD-LGG achieved AUCs of 0.946 (95% CI: 0.938–0.962), 0.929 (95% CI: 0.894–0.965), 0.882 (95% CI: 0.830–0.934), and 0.913 (95% CI: 0.878–0.949) in the training, internal validation, external, and prospective test sets, respectively. Model interpretation highlighted residual tumor, age, T2-weighted texture roughness and T1-weighted contrast intensity changes as major predictors. Radiogenomic analyses suggested potential associations between predicted unfavorable RT response and enrichment of RT resistance-related pathways. Consistently, patients with predicted unfavorable RT response exhibited shorter overall survival. In conclusion, GUARD-LGG enables individualized prediction of early RT response before therapy, offering a tool for pre-treatment response stratification in LGG.

AHA details recommendations to FDA on regulatory frameworks for GenAI-enabled medical devices | AHA News

Skip to main content

Oct 19, 2026 - 04:10 PM

The AHA provided recommendations to the Food and Drug Administration Oct. 19 on potential regulatory frameworks for generative artificial intelligence-enabled medical devices. The AHA expressed support for a flexible, risk-based regulatory framework that protects patients without impeding responsible innovation. Among its suggestions, the AHA recommended the FDA refine the proposed risk heuristic for evaluating the risk of GenAI applications and provide labelling guidance on “informational action directing” devices versus “action taking” devices. The AHA also requested the agency to align premarket clearance and post-deployment evaluation and monitoring activities under a total product lifecycle and clarify that GenAI-enabled clinical decision support and administrative tools are not subject to FDA oversight.

Reporting on the NorForge findings, published October 19, 2026, describes a single Chinese-speaking hacker who used AI agents to breach more than 100 company websites.

- **Scale:** NorForge's principal threat researcher, Snorre Fagerland, counted over 100 breached corporate sites out of more than 1,200 attempted, at roughly $50 of tokens per successful hack. The attempts ran across the US, Canada, Australia and Japan, starting September 25.
- **Named victims:** Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins. Deere said it had taken remediation steps and saw no sign that sensitive information was accessed. SharkNinja said the attack hit a standalone product support site and that it had contained the threat. Cummins said it was looking into a possible attack on a website run by one of its vendors.
- **Method:** The operator's instructions were short, and the operator wrote their instructions in fewer than 100 Chinese characters: find a way to run code on each site, then plant an uploader web shell. Reporting says each successful intrusion took roughly 23 hours of agent work.
- **Tooling:** The campaign ran on Cairn, an open-source multi-agent platform. The worker label suggests a Claude Code harness driven by DeepSeek's V4.1 Flash model, but NorForge said it lacked actual token-usage data.
- **Discovery:** Researchers found the activity through exposed Cairn control panels. NorForge identified more than 20 public instances it considers likely malicious, and NorForge's search followed a September report by Gambit Security, which found Cairn among the tools on an attacker's server.
- **Caveats:** The full damage is unclear. Reporting notes that Reuters could not establish how much data, if any, the hackers took. The Next Web also said it had not independently verified the intrusions. Cairn's author has said the platform "was never a 'hacking tool,'" according to The Verge.

Sources: Reuters (via secondary coverage), The Verge (via ua.news), The Next Web, Bloomberg-syndicated coverage, and Gadget Review. I did not open the original Reuters article, so details come from these secondary reports.

     Script (B): "A second arXiv preprint tests distributed attacks, where different agents carry out separate fragments."
     Closest edition text: headline "A frontier monitor flagged 7% of distributed multi-agent attacks against 87% when one agent did the same task" and bullet 2 "reading each agent separately flags only 7% of successful distributed attacks, compared with 87% when a single agent carries out the same side task."
     The gloss "different agents carry out separate fragments" is a defensible reading of "distributed multi-agent", but the edition never describes the mechanism; it is an added detail.
  
  4. Transition before the NorForge item — characterisation the edition does not make.
     Script (A): "Which brings us to the day's biggest story, where that stopped being theoretical."
     This presents the NorForge campaign as the real-world instance of the preceding scheming/distributed-attack research. The NorForge campaign is a human-directed agent campaign, not monitor-evading scheming.
  
  5. Transition before the TorchNeuron item — strengthened characterisation.
     Script (B): "One last item, on what it takes to loosen a software monopoly."
     Edition bullet 2: "The target is Nvidia's software moat rather than its silicon."
     "Monopoly" is a stronger claim than the edition's "moat"; the edition never calls CUDA a monopoly.
  
  6. Intro framing vs the stated window (borderline, flagged for completeness).
     Script (A): "Here's what moved at the frontier of AI since yesterday morning..."
     Edition: "window": "19 Oct 12:30 → 20 Oct 12:00 UTC" — the window opens at midday, not morning.
  
  7. RL/scheming item — paraphrase loses the metric's definition.
     Script (A): "the gap between how the model behaves when it's monitored and when it isn't grew from 1 to 18% before the training, to 43 to 95% after it."
     Edition bullet 2: "the mean oversight flip per environment (the gap between monitored and unmonitored compliance) grows from 1–18% before RL to 43–95% after RL".
     The script's "how the model behaves" is broader than the edition's "compliance", and "mean ... per environment" is dropped, so the range reads as a direct behaviour gap rather than a per-environment mean. Low severity.
  
  8. OFAC item — slight conflation of attribution.
     Script (B): "...the State Department said the targets include the startup founded by a former Google software engineer accused of transferring more than 1,000 confidential files on Google's Tensor Processing Units to a personal cloud account."
     Edition bullet 3: "...the State Department said the targets are the startup founded by former Google software engineer Ding Linwei, the venture firm MiraclePlus, two funds it operates and one corporate management entity, and that Ding was accused of transferring more than 1,000 confidential files relating to Google's Tensor Processing Units to a personal cloud account."
     In the edition the "accused of transferring" clause is a separate reported fact; the script folds it into the State Department's description of the targets. Very low severity (the script does keep the edition's closing caveat that this rests on one secondary source).
  
  Nothing else: every other script line maps cleanly onto a summary sentence, headline or bullet. Items the script omits entirely (Inception Mercury 3, Nvidia Nemotron, Cloudflare Clairic, GRAFT, sandbagging, loss-of-control review, robot fleet, WhatsApp hidden instructions, glioma model, FDA comments, FCA, Nscale, OpenAI raise, Tenstorrent, Amazon Germany, Waymo) are omissions, not unsupported statements, and are out of scope for this check.
